tables.how: City payee names since fiscal 2019 are matched on a normalised key (legal suffixes, punctuation and "DBA" removed) to the Treasurer’s business registry, the State contractor-licence file, tax-return related-organization schedules and State cannabis licences. Tier 1: two names under one owner account or one ownership name (for a personal ownership name, only accounts that also share an address). Tier 2: one State person number current on both licences. Tier 3: a filing names one as trade name, parent, subsidiary or related organization of the other. Tier 4: same suite-level address and the same telephone or named owner. Groups are built from tiers 1 to 4 only; tiers 5 and 6 never chain and are shown as pairs. An address is used only if no more than 4 owners were ever registered at the suite (or 8 at a building with no suite written), and owners with more than 10 sites are left out. Here every set is given in full, ordered as the analysis orders them (tier, then the amount paid to the second name), with one row per payee name: 709 names in 300 sets. The tie printed is the chain of records from the set’s largest name to this one, strongest first; for a tier 5 pair the tie between the two sides is the shared address. The case’s "paid under second and later names" is the set’s payments less its largest name, added over the 101 sets on record evidence.
tables.limits: One owner running several businesses is ordinary, and the City may knowingly pay a parent and its subsidiary, a firm under its old and new name after a merger or renaming, or a nonprofit and the housing partnerships it sponsors (the tier 3 rows declared on a tax return are disclosed by the organizations themselves). The question for a reader is narrower: whether two names were treated as two parties where a rule assumes separate parties; that rule should be checked for each row, because none is stated in these files. Names are matched exactly after normalising, so a common name can pick the wrong company and a misspelt one is missed. The registry names an owner, not officers or shareholders. A name that reads as a private individual’s is replaced by a code; that test uses lists of given and family names from the State licence, City payroll and tax-return files and can miss an unusual name. Many tier 5 rows read as a joint venture and one of its own members, a landlord and tenant, or a manager and a building it runs. A tier 5 row is a lead, not a record of common ownership.

tables.how: Purchase orders under the departments’ delegated authority (the file’s "Prop Q" authority), each between $2,500 and the limit in force that year, are grouped by department and owner-group. A cluster is two or more differently named vendors of one group (or one address pair) with orders dated within 14 days of the first, whose amounts add up to more than the limit. The limit is taken from the “split purchases” results: Delegated ("Prop Q") purchasing limit: $10,000 through FY2024, $20,000 from FY2025. "Just under" counts orders in the top tenth below the limit. One row is one department and one set of vendors; the largest single cluster is written out. Here every order in every cluster is listed (63 orders in 19 clusters). 69,068 delegated orders at or under the limit were tested.
tables.limits: The limit is stated in these files per purchase order; whether related vendors must be counted together is not stated and should be checked against the purchasing rules. Two affiliated firms can sell different things, as several of the names suggest, and a department may need both in one fortnight. Several of these rows also show repeated orders to one of the two names alone, which the “split purchases” results already measures. Orders are matched to firms by payee name. The purchase-order extract holds only orders totalling $2,500 to $25,000.

tables.how: A pool is one department’s contract title that contains "as-needed", "pool", "on-call", "pre-qualified", "job order" or "master agreement" and has at least 3 different prime contractors in the Controller’s contract file. Every pair of primes is tested against the owner-groups and address leads, and against the file’s own list of joint-venture members. The share is the tied members’ payments over all payments under that title; agreed amounts are shown beside them. Every prime contractor of the 50 pools is listed (205); agreed and paid amounts add up every line of the contract file under the title for that prime, as the analysis does.
tables.limits: Pools are found from contract titles, so differently titled rounds of one pool are separate rows and pools with other wording are missed. Whether a firm may hold a place alone and also through a joint venture in the same pool is set by the solicitation, which is not in these files and should be checked. Subcontractors are ignored: a pool member working as another member’s subcontractor is common and is not counted. Payments recorded as zero mean the file shows none, not that no work was done.

tables.how: Each published tabulation is one list (the same grouping as the bid screens in the site’s “Earmarks, bids and other public bodies” page). Every pair of bidders on a list is tested against the owner-groups (tiers 1 to 4) and the address leads (tiers 5 and 6). The gap shown is from the lower of the two tied bids to the next bid from a firm outside the pair. The recommended bidder is the one named for award in the same agenda item. None of the 108 bid lists carries two bidders that these files tie to one owner-group, one State-licensed person or one address. Of the 121 bidder names, 90 were found in the City business registry and 89 on a State contractor licence, so the test could see most but not all of the field.
tables.limits: The sample is 108 bid lists from Public Works, the Port and Muni; the notes with the bid files record that the airport and the water department publish none without a login. Affiliated firms may bid separately where the bid rules allow it; whether a bid list forbids related bidders is in the bid documents, which are not in these files and should be checked. Bid sheets give no address, licence number or owner, so bidders are tied to records by name only; a bidder registered under another name is missed. The State file leaves out revoked and cancelled licences.

tables.title: Licence lists, drawings and grant rounds: every name the case counts as one owner in more than one place
tables.what: One name (or, for a private individual, the analysis’s code) in a drawing, licence list or grant round that the files tie to another entry of the same owner, or that holds more than one entry under one name.

tables.how: Each file is tested for the same party appearing more than once: by name within the file, by owner-group (tiers 1 to 4) and by address lead (tiers 5 and 6). For the condominium lottery, which lists buildings and not owners, each building’s address is matched to registry owners that had a property business registered there in the lottery year; an owner counts only with two or more buildings in one drawing. Private individuals are shown as codes made from a hash; businesses and organizations are named. Rows on record evidence come first, then address matches, then name matches. Condominium lottery (2001 to 2013): 1,996 buildings made 6,987 entries and 818 wins; 7 building(s) show as a winner twice, and 2 registry owner(s) had a property business at two or more buildings entered in one drawing. Taxi medallions: 18 of 801 holder names hold more than one of the 1,145 medallions, the largest being SFFCU (San Francisco Federal Credit Union) Taxi Medallion Holder with 292. Cannabis: 17 owner-group(s) hold State licences under two or more legal names, and 60 more pairs share only an owner’s name. Grant rounds: 8 pair(s) of tied organizations were funded in the same round. Mobile food and street vending: 1 group(s) under two applicant names; 4 vending names appear twice.
tables.limits: The drawing results and published rules downloaded to the project's saved copy (not hosted here) are analysed separately (the site’s “Drawings and repeat winners” page), which also reads the owner-groups written here; this screen uses only the files named in its sources and quotes no rule, so which of these lists allows one entry per party should be checked before any row is read as a problem. A registry owner at a lottery building’s address may be a manager or a shop, not the applicant; the Assessor’s public roll does not name owners. The taxi and permit files show only current holders, with no history, and the same printed name can be two people. The two largest medallion holders are credit unions; the file does not say how they came to hold them. The City’s cannabis equity list, housing-lottery applicants and street-space drawings are not published. Surname-and-address matching (tier 6) could not be run on files that give no address. Cannabis owners, taxi drivers and vendors who are private people are not named; the pairs of cannabis legal names that share only an owner’s name are listed by legal name with the owner left out.

tables.how: Local-business status is the "LBE" flag the Controller’s contract file prints beside each prime contractor, subcontractor and joint-venture member. Each flagged name is looked up in the owner-groups (tiers 1 to 4) and address leads (tier 5). A tie is listed when the other name does not carry the flag and either was paid at least $5 million and five times as much as the flagged firm since fiscal 2019, or is registered in the business registry only at addresses outside California. Here every tie of the 135 flagged names that have one is listed (163 rows); the case counts the 4 marked in the last column.
tables.limits: The size and ownership limits for local-business certification are not in any file on disk and should be checked before reading a row as a problem; a certified firm may share an office with, or be a joint-venture partner of, a large firm, and most tier 5 rows are exactly that. The flag is as recorded on each contract and may predate or postdate a change of ownership. The City’s certified-firm directory with owners, and the State directory of disadvantaged businesses (behind a CAPTCHA), are not on disk.

sources.t: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, provider enrolment "All Owners" files

tables.how: From the federal enrolment owners extract already used by the “health” results, only rows where the owner holds an ownership interest or is a partner are kept (officers, directors and managing employees are dropped). Owners are identified by the federal owner number, not by name. Providers are gathered into one group wherever an owner number appears on two of them, so a chain held through layers of holding companies is one row; a group is listed if it has two or more differently named enrolments in the Bay Area counties and at least one in San Francisco. Billing numbers are the distinct provider, certification and enrolment numbers in the set. 6 groups of two or more differently named Bay Area providers, each with at least one San Francisco address, are joined by owner numbers in the federal enrolment file; 4 have two or more names in San Francisco itself and 1 have two names at one street address. The largest holds 32 provider names and 96 billing numbers (Bay Area Master Tenant Llc; Bay Bridge Capital Partners, Llc; Hudson River Opco Llc; Pacs Group, Inc. and 4 more organizations). 3 of the groups include an owner already on the list in the “health” results; what this screen adds is the restriction to ownership interests and the count of names and billing numbers per group.
tables.limits: Chains are disclosed to Medicare in exactly this file, so nothing here is hidden from the payer; the screen shows where separate provider names and numbers are one business, which matters when reading the address clusters in the “health” results and the site’s “Hospices, nursing homes and prescribers” page. Only provider types with an ownership file on disk are covered (nursing homes, home health agencies, hospices, hospitals, and federally qualified and rural health clinics); physician groups, pharmacies, laboratories and equipment suppliers have none. Individuals are shown as codes. Some provider names in the federal extract are garbled (for example names ending "idence Opco") and are printed as the file gives them; the source looks wrong there, not the provider.

tables.limits: A shared suite is often a landlord and tenant, a joint venture and its member, or a manager and the building it runs. Leads never chain, and nothing here says the two sides have one owner.
